newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan May bankruptcies surge 46.7 pct yr/yr.
newsitem.headline: Japan May bankruptcies surge 46.7 pct yr/yr.

text.p: Total debts held by Japanese companies that went bankrupt in May surged 46.7 percent from a year earlier to 487.70 billion yen, continuing the sharp rising trend since early this year, a research firm said on Friday.
The total number of Japanese companies that failed in May rose by 1.2 percent from a year earlier to 1,331, Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd said.

"Bankruptcies have clearly entered a period of growth at the beginning of this year. Small- and medium-sized companies suffering from the burst of the economic 'bubble' are likely to face further difficulties," Tokyo Shoko said.
Debts held by Japanese companies which went under since the beginning of this year already totalled more than 5.9 trillion yen, more than six percent larger that total annual debts in calendar 1994.
Average debts at a failed company were 901 million yen during the first five months of 1997, against 400 million yen for the same period last year.
The increase in 1997 is largely due to failure of companies hit by the burst of the economic bubble in the early 1990s.
Bankruptices are expected at about 7,800 cases during the six months to June 30, 1997, compared to 7,270 cases in the same period the year ago, Tokyo Shoko said.

"Although a slight recovery is seen in the economy led by brisk business at exporters, domestic demand-related industries, such as department stores and chainstores, suffered from stagnant individual consumption," Tokyo Shoko said.

Debts held by failed firms in May was the third largest on record for the month but 81.3 percent lower than April, as April faced total debts of 2.03 trillion yen by three nonbank financial firms, Tokyo Shoko said.
The firms were Crown Leasing Corp, Nippon Total Finance Inc, and Nippon Assurance Finance Services Co, all affiliated with troubled long-term credit bank Nippon Credit Bank Ltd.
Tokyo Shoko said 59.3 percent of the failures in May were recession-related, such as sluggish sales, accumulated losses and difficulty in recovering credit sales.

Retailers and wholesalers were hit hard by a drop in individual consumption following a rise in consumption tax to five percent from three percent which took effect on April 1. Bankruptcies of retailers rose 23.7 percent to 177 cases, and failures of wholesalers stood at 271 cases, up 5.4 percent year-on-year.
There were five companies which went under in the financial and insurance industry in May, compared to three companies a year ago.
